items.title: A name the registry would not accept
items.dek: In a new essay for Literary Hub, the novelist Kirmen Uribe argues that a minority language survives by being chosen, not by being kept pure, and that a small literature can be a stage as easily as a cage.
paragraphs: Kirmen Uribe's life as a writer begins, by his own account, at a civil registry counter. He was born in the Basque Country in the early 1970s, while Franco was still in power, and the clerk who recorded his birth told his mother that Basque names were not permitted, offering Spanish alternatives instead. She refused to give way, and the official record still carries the single name Kirmen. For Uribe, who recounts the episode in an essay published by Literary Hub on 9 November, the scene contains the whole problem of a minority language in miniature: a word that is ordinary at home becomes an act of defiance the moment it meets the state.

What follows is less a lament than an inventory of recovery. Uribe belongs, he writes, to the first generation that could be educated in Basque from primary school all the way to university, in a system that began in improvised classrooms before it had printed textbooks, and that was soon joined by Basque-language radio and television. He puts the number of speakers today at around one million in a region of almost two and a half million, and notes that roughly a third more people speak the language than did in the 1970s. Many of them, he stresses, learned it as adults, and he counts them as Basque speakers by adoption rather than as second-class heirs.

That emphasis on adoption is the essay's quiet polemic. Basque is famous as a linguistic isolate, a language that predates the Indo-European arrivals in Europe, and it is tempting to romanticise it as a sealed survivor of deep time. Uribe declines the temptation. He delights instead in the words Basque has borrowed over the centuries from Latin, Arabic, French and Spanish, down to a verb for googling, and he recalls how his own student theory about an ancient sound in the speech of his home town, Ondarroa, collapsed when it turned out to come from older speakers' dentures. A living language, on this account, is defined by traffic, not by purity.

The political edge of the argument lies in what Uribe says about smallness. A minor literature, he suggests, can make its writers visible far beyond their numbers, yet it can just as easily turn them into emblems, with institutions anointing one figure as the representative voice and expecting loyalty in return. He sets Claudio Magris's view that border cultures see the world with unusual sharpness against Milan Kundera's warning that small nations may demand obedience from their artists. The tension is familiar to anyone who has watched identity become a brand: the same recognition that protects a culture can also fence its writers in.

Uribe's own life now complicates the picture further. He lives in New York and teaches at New York University, speaking Basque at home and Spanish in the classroom, in a city he describes as home to more than six hundred languages. He writes in Basque, Spanish and English, and resists calling this self-translation, preferring the idea of writing oneself anew in each language. His novel Life Before Dolphins, translated from Spanish by Megan McDowell and published in English by Coffee House Press, won the Spanish Critics Award for narrative in Basque in 2022.

Read from the left, the essay offers a useful corrective to two opposite habits. Against the nationalist instinct to treat a minority tongue as blood inheritance, Uribe makes belonging a matter of practice and choice, open to newcomers and learners. Against a cosmopolitanism that shrugs at small languages as quaint, he shows how much institutional effort, from schools to broadcasters, it took to make one viable again. It is a reminder that linguistic survival is as much a question of public investment as of private loyalty, which is, he notes at the end, what his name means.

glossary.en: on a small scale that nonetheless contains all the features of something larger
to yield under pressure or stop resisting
a forceful argument against an opinion or position
a language with no demonstrable relationship to any other living language
glossary.zh: 孤立语言（无亲属关系的语言）

glossary.en: to present something as more ideal or heroic than it is
to choose someone formally or symbolically as a leader or representative
to confine or restrict someone's freedom of movement or action
something that counteracts or puts right a mistaken tendency
to treat something as unimportant or not worth concern
able to survive and function successfully

items.grammar: Paragraph four says a minor literature can make writers visible 'yet it can just as easily turn them into emblems'. 'Just as easily' (and the parallel 'as much a question of X as of Y' in the last paragraph) is a comparative of equality used concessively: it grants the first claim while insisting the opposite outcome is equally likely or important. The structure lets a writer refuse a one-sided reading without explicitly saying 'but'.
items.grammar_zh: 第四段说小语种文学能让作家被看见，“yet it can just as easily turn them into emblems”。“just as easily”以及最后一段的“as much a question of X as of Y”都是同级比较，这里带让步意味：先承认前一种说法，再强调相反的结果同样可能或同样重要。这样写不必直接用“but”，就能拒绝片面的解读。
questions: Why does Uribe treat adult learners as full Basque speakers, and what does this imply about how cultural belonging should be defined?
How can the visibility granted to a 'small literature' become a constraint on its writers? Think of an example from another language or culture.
The final paragraph claims that language survival depends on public investment as much as private loyalty. Do you agree?

sources.title: Kirmen Uribe, 'What It Means To Be a Basque Writer', Literary Hub, 9 November 2026

items.title: The steelpan: how old oil drums learned to sing
items.dek: A bright, bell-like instrument born in the streets of Trinidad.
paragraphs: Imagine a musical instrument made from a metal barrel. It sounds sweet, bright and a little like a bell. This is the steelpan, and it comes from the islands of Trinidad and Tobago in the Caribbean.

The story of the steelpan began in the street. In the early twentieth century, Carnival groups called tamboo bamboo bands were making rhythms with bamboo sticks. Later, the musicians added pieces of metal, such as a car's brake part and a biscuit tin. The steelpan grew out of these bands during the 1930s and 1940s.

Nobody can name one single inventor. While some players were testing old pots and pans, others were trying oil drums, and they all kept learning from each other. Today, a modern pan is made from a 200-litre industrial drum. The maker shapes the top into several ovals, and each oval is one note: the bigger the oval, the lower the sound. Then a tuner works carefully with small hammers until every note is right.

Two names are famous in this story. Ellie Mannette is often called the 'Father of the Modern Steel Drum', and Winston 'Spree' Simon is known for the 'Ping Pong' pan, a lead instrument that plays the tune. In 1951, both men travelled to Britain with the Trinidad All-Steel Pan Percussion Orchestra, a band that came to play at the Festival of Britain.

Steelbands are not small. In Trinidad, big orchestras sometimes have over a hundred players, and every year they take part in Panorama, which Wikipedia describes as the largest steelband contest in the world. In Britain, there has been a Panorama at the Notting Hill Carnival in London since 1978. If you walk through the streets of Notting Hill at the end of August, you might hear a steel orchestra practising before the contest.

In 2023, the United Nations General Assembly declared 11 August to be World Steelpan Day. It is a proud moment for an instrument that began on the streets with ordinary objects. Next time you see an old metal drum, look at it again: it could be the start of a song.
paragraphs_zh: 想象一种用金属桶做成的乐器。它的声音甜美、明亮，有点像钟声。这就是钢鼓（steelpan），它来自加勒比海的特立尼达和多巴哥群岛。
钢鼓的故事始于街头。二十世纪初，狂欢节上有一种叫“tamboo bamboo”的竹乐队，用竹棒敲出节奏。后来，乐手们加入了金属物件，比如汽车的刹车部件和饼干铁盒。钢鼓就是在二十世纪三四十年代从这些乐队中发展出来的。
没有人能说出唯一的发明者。当一些乐手在试验旧锅旧盘的时候，另一些人在试验油桶，大家不断互相学习。今天，现代钢鼓是用200升的工业桶制成的。制作者把桶面塑造成若干个椭圆，每个椭圆就是一个音：椭圆越大，声音越低。然后调音师用小锤子仔细地敲，直到每个音都准确。
这个故事里有两个著名的名字。埃利·曼内特（Ellie Mannette）常被称为“现代钢鼓之父”，温斯顿“斯普里”西蒙（Winston ‘Spree’ Simon）则以“乒乓”（Ping Pong）鼓闻名，这是一种演奏旋律的主音鼓。1951年，两人随特立尼达全钢鼓打击乐团前往英国，这个乐团是去参加英国节（Festival of Britain）演出的。
钢鼓乐队并不小。在特立尼达，大型乐团有时有一百多名乐手，每年他们都参加“Panorama”，维基百科称它为世界上最大的钢鼓乐队比赛。在英国，自1978年起，伦敦的诺丁山狂欢节上也有了Panorama。如果你八月底走在诺丁山的街头，也许会听到钢鼓乐团在比赛前练习。
2023年，联合国大会宣布8月11日为“世界钢鼓日”。对一件从街头用普通物件开始的乐器来说，这是一个自豪的时刻。下次你看到一只旧金属桶时，再看它一眼：它也许就是一首歌的开始。

glossary.en: a tall plant with hard, hollow stems
a large metal container for oil
to change an instrument so each note sounds right
a shape like a long circle, or an egg
a large group of musicians who play together
a competition where people try to win
a regular pattern of beats in music
to grow or change slowly into something new
to join an activity with other people

items.grammar: Past simple vs past continuous: use the past simple for finished actions (“The steelpan grew out of these bands”) and the past continuous (was/were + -ing) for an action in progress, often in the background (“While some players were testing old pots and pans, others were trying oil drums”). “While” often goes with the past continuous.
items.grammar_zh: 一般过去时 vs 过去进行时：已经完成的动作用一般过去时（“The steelpan grew out of these bands”）；某个时间段内正在进行的动作、常作背景，用过去进行时 was/were + -ing（“While some players were testing old pots and pans, others were trying oil drums”，一些乐手在试验旧锅旧盘时，另一些人在试验油桶）。while 常和过去进行时连用。
questions: Where does the steelpan come from, and what is a modern pan made from?
What does the size of an oval tell you about its note?
What do you think: could you make music from everyday objects in your home? Which ones?

items.title: En el Malecón de La Habana: de niña yo vivía…
items.dek: Dos vecinas conversan junto al mar en La Habana y se cuentan cómo era su vida de niñas.
paragraphs: Yamila: ¡Hola, Marta! ¿Qué tal? ¿Qué haces aquí tan temprano?
Marta: Hola, Yamila. Estoy mirando el mar. De niña venía al Malecón todos los domingos.
Yamila: ¿De verdad? ¿Dónde vivías entonces?
Marta: Vivía en un barrio cerca de aquí, con mis abuelos. Mi casa era pequeña, pero muy alegre.
Yamila: ¿Y qué hacías los domingos?
Marta: Primero íbamos a la playa. Mi abuelo pescaba y yo jugaba con mis primos.
Yamila: ¡Qué bonito! ¿Y tu abuela?
Marta: Ella siempre preparaba el almuerzo. Cocinaba arroz con frijoles y plátanos fritos.
Yamila: ¡Yo también comía eso en casa! Me encantaba.
Marta: ¿Y tú? ¿Dónde vivías de pequeña?
Yamila: Vivía en Santiago de Cuba. Mi escuela estaba lejos y caminaba una hora todos los días.
Marta: ¡Una hora! ¿No te cansabas?
Yamila: Un poco, pero iba con mis amigas y hablábamos todo el camino.
Marta: ¡Qué recuerdos! ¿Quieres tomar un café conmigo?
Yamila: ¡Claro! Vamos.
Dato curioso: en Cuba muchas personas saludan con «¿Qué bolá?», que significa más o menos «¿Qué tal?». Y para el autobús dicen «la guagua».
paragraphs_en: Yamila: Hi, Marta! How are you? What are you doing here so early?
Marta: Hi, Yamila. I'm looking at the sea. As a child I came to the Malecón every Sunday.
Yamila: Really? Where did you live then?
Marta: I lived in a neighborhood near here, with my grandparents. My house was small, but very cheerful.
Yamila: And what did you do on Sundays?
Marta: First we went to the beach. My grandfather fished and I played with my cousins.
Yamila: How lovely! And your grandmother?
Marta: She always made lunch. She cooked rice with beans and fried plantains.
Yamila: I ate that at home too! I loved it.
Marta: And you? Where did you live as a little girl?
Yamila: I lived in Santiago de Cuba. My school was far away and I walked an hour every day.
Marta: An hour! Weren't you tired?
Yamila: A little, but I went with my friends and we talked the whole way.
Marta: What memories! Do you want to have a coffee with me?
Yamila: Of course! Let's go.
Fun fact: in Cuba many people greet each other with “¿Qué bolá?”, which means roughly “How's it going?”. And for the bus they say “la guagua”.
paragraphs_de: Yamila: Hallo, Marta! Wie geht's? Was machst du so früh hier?
Marta: Hallo, Yamila. Ich schaue aufs Meer. Als Kind kam ich jeden Sonntag zum Malecón.
Yamila: Wirklich? Wo hast du damals gewohnt?
Marta: Ich wohnte in einem Viertel ganz in der Nähe, bei meinen Großeltern. Unser Haus war klein, aber sehr fröhlich.
Yamila: Und was hast du sonntags gemacht?
Marta: Zuerst gingen wir zum Strand. Mein Opa angelte und ich spielte mit meinen Cousins.
Yamila: Wie schön! Und deine Oma?
Marta: Sie machte immer das Mittagessen. Sie kochte Reis mit Bohnen und gebratene Kochbananen.
Yamila: Das habe ich zu Hause auch gegessen! Ich liebte es.
Marta: Und du? Wo hast du als Kind gewohnt?
Yamila: Ich wohnte in Santiago de Cuba. Meine Schule war weit weg und ich lief jeden Tag eine Stunde.
Marta: Eine Stunde! Warst du nicht müde?
Yamila: Ein bisschen, aber ich ging mit meinen Freundinnen und wir redeten den ganzen Weg.
Marta: Was für Erinnerungen! Möchtest du mit mir einen Kaffee trinken?
Yamila: Klar! Gehen wir.
Wissenswertes: In Kuba grüßen sich viele mit „¿Qué bolá?“, das heißt ungefähr „Wie läuft's?“. Und für den Bus sagt man „la guagua“.
items.grammar: The imperfect (imperfecto) describes how things used to be and what you used to do regularly. Regular endings: -ar verbs take -aba (“jugaba”), -er/-ir verbs take -ía (“vivía”, “comía”). Only ir (iba), ser (era) and ver (veía) are irregular. Example: “Vivía en Santiago de Cuba.”
items.grammar_de: Das Imperfecto beschreibt, wie etwas früher war und was man regelmäßig tat. Regelmäßige Endungen: -ar-Verben haben -aba („jugaba“), -er/-ir-Verben haben -ía („vivía“, „comía“). Nur ir (iba), ser (era) und ver (veía) sind unregelmäßig. Beispiel: „Vivía en Santiago de Cuba.“
questions: ¿Dónde vivía Marta de niña y qué hacía los domingos?
¿Y tú? ¿Dónde vivías de niño o de niña y qué te gustaba hacer?

items.title: Matilde Hidalgo: la puerta cerrada que se abrió
items.dek: La primera bachiller, la primera médica y una de las primeras mujeres que votaron en América Latina: la historia de una ecuatoriana que insistió.
paragraphs: En octubre de 1913, en la ciudad ecuatoriana de Loja, una joven de veinticuatro años terminó el bachillerato y, sin saberlo, entró en los libros de historia. Se llamaba Matilde Hidalgo y fue la primera mujer de Ecuador que se graduó de la secundaria. Para lograrlo, había pedido con insistencia, con la ayuda de su hermano, que la aceptaran en un colegio laico de su ciudad, y después de un tiempo el director aceptó. Aquel «sí» cambió su destino y, con los años, también el de muchas otras mujeres.

El camino hacia la universidad no fue más fácil. En Quito, la Universidad Central no quiso admitirla porque era mujer y, según se cuenta, un decano le aconsejó que se dedicara a su casa y a sus futuros hijos. Matilde no se rindió. En 1919 viajó a Cuenca, estudió medicina allí y se graduó con honores. Dos años más tarde volvió a Quito y consiguió el doctorado, de modo que se convirtió en la primera médica del país. Además, escribía poemas desde sus años de estudiante, y esa afición la acompañó durante mucho tiempo.

El momento por el que más se la recuerda llegó en 1924. Cuando se acercaban las elecciones presidenciales, Matilde anunció que pensaba votar. En aquella época las mujeres no votaban, y mucha gente creía que la ley simplemente no lo permitía. Sin embargo, el asunto se llevó a una consulta oficial y la respuesta fue favorable. Así, en la ciudad de Machala, Matilde depositó su voto. Por eso se la considera la primera mujer latinoamericana que votó en unas elecciones nacionales, y Ecuador suele citarse entre los primeros países de la región que reconocieron el voto femenino.

Su vida pública no terminó ahí. Ejerció la medicina en Guayaquil, fue la primera mujer concejal de Machala y, en 1941, se presentó como candidata en Loja, su ciudad natal. Más tarde ganó una beca para estudiar pediatría y neurología en Argentina. Recibió varios reconocimientos nacionales por su trabajo y murió en Guayaquil en 1974, a los ochenta y cuatro años.

Hoy su historia sirve para pensar en lo que damos por sentado. Si Matilde viviera ahora, probablemente se alegraría de que las mujeres voten, estudien medicina y se presenten a las elecciones sin pedir permiso a nadie. Pero también preguntaría qué otras puertas siguen cerradas, y quizás nos pediría que no esperáramos a que otra persona las abriera. Si cada generación se conformara con lo que ya existe, nada cambiaría; por eso conviene recordar a quienes, hace cien años, insistieron en que una puerta cerrada no es una puerta cerrada para siempre.
Dato curioso: en 2019 Google le dedicó un Doodle a Matilde Hidalgo para recordar los 130 años de su nacimiento, y así su historia llegó a un público mucho más amplio.
paragraphs_en: In October 1913, in the Ecuadorian city of Loja, a 24-year-old woman finished secondary school and, without knowing it, entered the history books. Her name was Matilde Hidalgo, and she was the first woman in Ecuador to graduate from high school. To achieve this, she had insistently asked, with her brother's help, to be accepted at a secular school in her city, and after a while the director agreed. That “yes” changed her destiny and, over the years, the destiny of many other women too.

The road to university was no easier. In Quito, the Central University refused to admit her because she was a woman and, as the story goes, a dean advised her to devote herself to her home and her future children. Matilde did not give up. In 1919 she traveled to Cuenca, studied medicine there and graduated with honors. Two years later she went back to Quito and earned her doctorate, so she became the first woman doctor in the country. She also wrote poems from her student years, and that hobby stayed with her for a long time.

The moment she is best remembered for came in 1924. As the presidential elections approached, Matilde announced that she intended to vote. At that time women did not vote, and many people believed the law simply did not allow it. However, the matter was taken to an official consultation and the answer was favorable. So, in the city of Machala, Matilde cast her vote. For this reason she is considered the first Latin American woman to vote in a national election, and Ecuador is often cited among the first countries in the region to recognize women's suffrage.

Her public life did not end there. She practiced medicine in Guayaquil, was the first woman councilor of Machala and, in 1941, ran as a candidate in Loja, her hometown. Later she won a scholarship to study pediatrics and neurology in Argentina. She received several national honors for her work and died in Guayaquil in 1974, at the age of eighty-four.

Today her story helps us think about what we take for granted. If Matilde were alive now, she would probably be glad that women vote, study medicine and run for office without asking anyone's permission. But she would also ask which other doors are still closed, and she might ask us not to wait for someone else to open them. If every generation settled for what already exists, nothing would change; that is why it is worth remembering those who, a hundred years ago, insisted that a closed door is not closed forever.
Fun fact: in 2019 Google dedicated a Doodle to Matilde Hidalgo to mark 130 years since her birth, and her story reached a much wider audience.
paragraphs_de: Im Oktober 1913 beendete in der ecuadorianischen Stadt Loja eine 24-jährige Frau die Schule mit dem Abitur und kam, ohne es zu wissen, in die Geschichtsbücher. Sie hieß Matilde Hidalgo und war die erste Frau in Ecuador, die einen Sekundarschulabschluss machte. Um das zu erreichen, hatte sie mit Hilfe ihres Bruders beharrlich darum gebeten, an einer weltlichen Schule ihrer Stadt aufgenommen zu werden, und nach einiger Zeit stimmte der Direktor zu. Dieses „Ja“ veränderte ihr Schicksal und mit den Jahren auch das vieler anderer Frauen.

Der Weg zur Universität war nicht leichter. In Quito wollte die Zentraluniversität sie nicht aufnehmen, weil sie eine Frau war, und einem Bericht zufolge riet ihr ein Dekan, sich lieber um Haus und künftige Kinder zu kümmern. Matilde gab nicht auf. 1919 reiste sie nach Cuenca, studierte dort Medizin und schloss mit Auszeichnung ab. Zwei Jahre später kehrte sie nach Quito zurück und erwarb den Doktortitel, sodass sie die erste Ärztin des Landes wurde. Außerdem schrieb sie seit ihrer Studienzeit Gedichte, und dieses Hobby begleitete sie lange.

Der Moment, an den man sich am meisten erinnert, kam 1924. Als die Präsidentschaftswahlen näher rückten, kündigte Matilde an, dass sie wählen wolle. Damals wählten Frauen nicht, und viele glaubten, das Gesetz erlaube es einfach nicht. Doch die Frage wurde offiziell angefragt, und die Antwort fiel günstig aus. So gab Matilde in der Stadt Machala ihre Stimme ab. Deshalb gilt sie als die erste lateinamerikanische Frau, die bei einer nationalen Wahl wählte, und Ecuador wird oft unter den ersten Ländern der Region genannt, die das Frauenwahlrecht anerkannten.

Ihr öffentliches Leben endete damit nicht. Sie arbeitete als Ärztin in Guayaquil, war die erste Stadträtin von Machala und kandidierte 1941 in Loja, ihrer Heimatstadt. Später gewann sie ein Stipendium, um in Argentinien Pädiatrie und Neurologie zu studieren. Sie erhielt mehrere nationale Auszeichnungen für ihre Arbeit und starb 1974 in Guayaquil im Alter von 84 Jahren.

Heute regt ihre Geschichte dazu an, über das nachzudenken, was wir für selbstverständlich halten. Wenn Matilde heute lebte, würde sie sich wahrscheinlich freuen, dass Frauen wählen, Medizin studieren und kandidieren, ohne jemanden um Erlaubnis zu bitten. Aber sie würde auch fragen, welche anderen Türen noch verschlossen sind, und uns vielleicht bitten, nicht darauf zu warten, dass jemand anderes sie öffnet. Würde sich jede Generation mit dem Bestehenden zufriedengeben, würde sich nichts ändern; deshalb lohnt es sich, an die zu erinnern, die vor hundert Jahren darauf bestanden, dass eine geschlossene Tür nicht für immer geschlossen bleibt.
Wissenswertes: 2019 widmete Google Matilde Hidalgo ein Doodle zum 130. Jahrestag ihrer Geburt, und so erreichte ihre Geschichte ein viel größeres Publikum.
items.grammar: Unreal present conditions (B2): si + imperfect subjunctive, then the conditional. It describes something unlikely or imaginary now: “Si Matilde viviera ahora, probablemente se alegraría…” (If Matilde were alive now, she would probably be glad…). The imperfect subjunctive is formed from the ustedes preterite stem: vivieron → viviera, conformaron → conformara. Never put the conditional in the si-clause.
items.grammar_de: Irreale Bedingungen der Gegenwart (B2): si + Imperfecto de subjuntivo, dann das Konditional. Das drückt etwas Unwahrscheinliches oder Erfundenes für jetzt aus: „Si Matilde viviera ahora, probablemente se alegraría…“ (Wenn Matilde jetzt lebte, würde sie sich wahrscheinlich freuen…). Der Imperfecto de subjuntivo wird vom Stamm des Pretérito in der 3. Person Plural gebildet: vivieron → viviera, conformaron → conformara. Das Konditional steht nie im si-Satz.
questions: ¿Qué obstáculos encontró Matilde Hidalgo para estudiar y qué hizo para superarlos?
¿Por qué se recuerda tanto su voto de 1924?
Si pudieras hablar con Matilde Hidalgo, ¿qué le preguntarías? ¿Y qué puertas crees que siguen cerradas hoy?

items.title: WhatsApp: um gato laranja na minha cozinha
items.dek: A Ana está na livraria. A Dona Rosa manda uma mensagem: tem um visitante na cozinha dela — e ele está com fome!
paragraphs: Dona Rosa (14:05): Ana, tem um gato laranja na minha cozinha. É seu?
Ana (14:06): É o meu Tito, sim! O que ele faz aí?
Dona Rosa (14:07): Ele come a comida do Bolinha!
Ana (14:08): Desculpa! E onde está o seu Bolinha?
Dona Rosa (14:09): No sofá. A tigela dele está vazia.
Ana (14:10): Coitado! Às seis eu levo ração para ele.
Dona Rosa (14:12): Obrigada, querida! E o Tito? Agora ele dorme na cama do Bolinha.
paragraphs_en: Dona Rosa (14:05): Ana, there's an orange cat in my kitchen. Is it yours?
Ana (14:06): It's my Tito, yes! What is he doing there?
Dona Rosa (14:07): He's eating Bolinha's food!
Ana (14:08): Sorry! And where is your Bolinha?
Dona Rosa (14:09): On the sofa. His bowl is empty.
Ana (14:10): Poor thing! At six I'll bring him some dog food.
Dona Rosa (14:12): Thank you, dear! And Tito? Now he's sleeping in Bolinha's bed.
paragraphs_zh: 罗莎太太（14:05）：安娜，我的厨房里有一只橘猫。是你的吗？
安娜（14:06）：是我的蒂托，没错！它在那儿干什么？
罗莎太太（14:07）：它在吃小球的饭！
安娜（14:08）：对不起！那你的小球在哪儿？
罗莎太太（14:09）：在沙发上。它的碗空了。
安娜（14:10）：可怜的家伙！六点我给它带狗粮来。
罗莎太太（14:12）：谢谢你，亲爱的！那蒂托呢？现在它睡在小球的床上。
paragraphs_de: Dona Rosa (14:05): Ana, in meiner Küche ist eine orange Katze. Ist das deine?
Ana (14:06): Das ist mein Tito, ja! Was macht er da?
Dona Rosa (14:07): Er frisst Bolinhas Futter!
Ana (14:08): Entschuldigung! Und wo ist dein Bolinha?
Dona Rosa (14:09): Auf dem Sofa. Sein Napf ist leer.
Ana (14:10): Der Arme! Um sechs bringe ich ihm Hundefutter.
Dona Rosa (14:12): Danke, meine Liebe! Und Tito? Jetzt schläft er in Bolinhas Bett.

glossary.pt: Lugar perto de você. Aqui é perto de mim.
Um prato fundo. O cachorro come na tigela.
Não tem nada dentro. A tigela vazia não tem comida.

glossary.zh: 他的 / 她的（放在名词后）
glossary.pt: De + ele = dele. A tigela dele = a tigela do Bolinha.
Palavra para dizer: que pena, ele está mal.
A comida de cachorro e de gato.

items.grammar: Seu/sua means 'your' and goes before the noun: o seu Bolinha, a sua casa. For 'his' or 'her', Brazilians usually say dele/dela after the noun (de + ele, de + ela): a tigela dele (his bowl), a cozinha dela (her kitchen).
items.grammar_zh: seu/sua 表示“你的”，放在名词前：o seu Bolinha，a sua casa。表示“他的 / 她的”，巴西人常把 dele/dela 放在名词后（de + ele，de + ela）：a tigela dele（它的碗），a cozinha dela（她的厨房）。
items.grammar_de: Seu/sua heißt „dein“ und steht vor dem Nomen: o seu Bolinha, a sua casa. Für „sein“ oder „ihr“ sagt man in Brasilien meist dele/dela nach dem Nomen (de + ele, de + ela): a tigela dele (sein Napf), a cozinha dela (ihre Küche).
items.grammar_pt: Seu e sua = de você: o seu Bolinha, a sua casa. Para ele e ela, a gente fala dele e dela depois da palavra: a tigela dele, a cozinha dela.
